warmup.q: A fraud model never sees a customer's ethnicity or neighbourhood. Its inputs are device, payment velocity, amount, and a postcode risk score learned from past chargeback investigations. Can it still treat two groups of customers differently?
options: No: without the group column it has nothing to discriminate on
Only if someone mislabeled the training data on purpose
Yes: the postcode score can carry the history of who was investigated, and stand in for the group
Only if one group really commits more fraud
warmup.why: If investigators used to check some neighbourhoods far more often, those postcodes carry more recorded fraud, and a score learned from the records flags their residents more, whatever they actually do. In this lesson's demo, both groups commit fraud at the same 1% rate and the model never sees the group, yet honest customers in one group are falsely flagged 8.3% of the time against 2.3% in the other.

sections.h: Automated decisions repeat the past, and someone has to answer for them
sections.html:
In 2016 ProPublica followed more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida, who had been scored by COMPAS, a tool that predicts whether someone will reoffend. Among those who did not reoffend within two years, 44.9% of Black defendants had been labelled higher risk, against 23.5% of white defendants. The errors in the other direction ran the other way: 47.7% of white defendants who did reoffend had been labelled lower risk, against 28.0% of Black defendants.

In 2019 Obermeyer and colleagues looked at a care-management algorithm from Optum, used to pick patients for extra help. It predicted future health costs as a stand-in for health needs. Less money is spent on Black patients with the same illnesses, so the model scored them as healthier than they were. Predicting need instead of cost would have raised the share of Black patients picked for extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%.

The mechanism is the same in both. A model learns from records of past decisions and past spending, not from the truth, and a proxy (a postcode, a cost, an IP address) carries the group into the model after the group column is removed. This lesson's demo builds a fraud model that never sees the group. Both groups commit fraud at the same rate, but one group's postcodes were investigated more in the past. Honest customers in that group are falsely flagged 8.3% of the time, against 2.3% in the other. You only see that if you measure error rates per group, which means knowing the group for evaluation, itself sensitive data that needs care.

Predictions also change the data the next model learns from. Flag more payments in one area, investigate more there, record more fraud there, and the postcode score rises again. Prices can loop too: a study of German petrol stations (Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, 2020 working paper) found that in two-station markets, margins didn't change when one station adopted algorithmic pricing and rose 28% when both did.

Then comes accountability: who answers when the system is wrong? On 21 August 2026 the Dutch data protection authority fined Uber €824,990,000, the second-largest GDPR fine so far, for deactivating drivers' accounts from 2018 to 2022 by fully automated decisions, on suspected fraud or low ratings, with no human review, and for not telling drivers about the automated decisions and profiling. Uber is appealing. GDPR Article 22 gives people the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, apart from some exceptions that still require safeguards such as a human who can review the decision. For a data system, that means a record of each decision with its inputs, model version and reasons, a review queue staffed by people who can overturn it, and a way for the person to contest it and correct the data it used. Vendors aren't safe either: in Mobley v. Workday, a US court let age-discrimination claims against an AI hiring-screening vendor proceed as a collective action in May 2025, though no court has ruled on the merits as of November 2026.

try.title: A model that never sees the group
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It is an invented example built to show one mechanism: 20,000 card payments, 30% from neighbourhood B, real fraud at 1% in both groups, and a model that flags the riskiest 5%.

Model A adds a postcode risk score, learned from past investigations that checked B's postcodes far more often, to a behaviour score. Model B uses behaviour only. Predict: which model treats honest customers in A and B differently, and does dropping the postcode cost much fraud caught?
Look at caught for both models. What would you need to know about each payment to even notice the difference in false positives?

code.title: FairnessDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val postcode = (if (b) 0.6 else 0.3) + 0.1 * gauss() // reflects past investigations, not fraud val behaviour = (if (fraud) 1.5 else 0.0) + 0.5 * gauss() // device, velocity, amount: real signal report("model A: postcode risk + behaviour (no group column)", payments) { it.postcodeRisk + it.behaviour } report("model B: behaviour only", payments) { it.behaviour }

try.expect:
-- model A: postcode risk + behaviour (no group column)
   group  payments  fraud  caught  false alarms  false-positive rate
   A         14068    149     127           325                 2.3%
   B          5932     62      59           489                 8.3%
-- model B: behaviour only
   group  payments  fraud  caught  false alarms  false-positive rate
   A         14068    149     133           560                 4.0%
   B          5932     62      55           252                 4.3%

Model A never reads the group, yet an honest customer in B is more than three times as likely to have a payment blocked. Model B treats the two groups about the same, and it catches 188 frauds against model A's 186. To see any of this you need the group of each payment at evaluation time, which is the uncomfortable part: measuring fairness needs the sensitive data you were trying not to use. The numbers are from a simulation, not a study; the mechanism is the one ProPublica and Obermeyer found.

sections.h: Privacy is a decision right, and personal data is a liability
sections.html:
A payments company sees every purchase: the pharmacy, the clinic, the bar, the betting site, the donation. Card data can reveal someone's health, religion, sexuality and debts without anyone ever typing those words. When a system stores what a user entered for their own purpose, the user is the customer. When it also records behaviour as a side effect and uses it for someone else (advertising, scoring, resale), the user becomes the subject of surveillance.

Privacy isn't secrecy. It is the right to decide what to reveal, to whom, and for what. Tracking moves that decision from the person to whoever holds the data. A privacy setting usually controls what other users can see, and says little about what the company does with the data itself.

Consent is the obvious answer, and it's weaker than it looks. Under the GDPR, consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give, so a pre-ticked box doesn't count. It is also only one of six legal bases; fraud prevention, for example, usually rests on legitimate interests or a legal obligation instead. In practice, few users can know what a dataset will be joined with, data about one person reveals others (contacts, relatives), and saying no to a service everyone else uses has a real cost.

Data is also a liability. 23andMe collected the genetic data of more than 13 million customers. A credential-stuffing attack in 2023 exposed customers' data, and the UK Information Commissioner later fined the company £2.31 million. The company filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, and a court approved the sale of its assets, the genetic data included, to TTAM Research Institute for $305 million. 27 states and the District of Columbia sued over consent. People who mailed a saliva sample to one company found their DNA sold as an asset of a bankrupt one. Data outlives the company that collected it, its promises and its owners.

So collect less. The GDPR's principles say it plainly: purpose limitation (use data only for the purposes it was collected for), data minimization (collect only what those purposes need) and storage limitation (keep it no longer than they need). Data you don't hold can't leak, can't be demanded by a court and can't be sold in a bankruptcy. Aggregate at ingest when a feature needs only totals, give every dataset a retention period by default, and pseudonymize where analysis doesn't need identity. A pseudonymized record is still personal data, because someone can still link it back.

try.title: Minimize one payment event
steps: A new feature shows each customer their monthly spending by category. The team proposes to consume the full payment event: card number, cardholder name, email, IP address, device fingerprint, GPS location, merchant ID, merchant category code, amount, currency, timestamp and the basket's line items.
Decide which fields the feature needs, which it can do without, and what you would store instead of raw events.
Write the retention period you'd give the stored data.
try.expect: It needs a customer key (a pseudonymous ID, not the card number or the email), the merchant category code, the amount, the currency and the month. It doesn't need the card number, name, email, IP address, device fingerprint, location, merchant ID or basket items. Store a running total per (customer key, month, category) instead of copies of the events: a few hundred bytes per customer per month instead of every payment. The totals are still personal data, since they are tied to a customer key, so give them a retention period that matches the feature (say 13 months, to show a year against the year before) and delete the row when the customer leaves. If the team later wants the basket items, that's a new purpose, and it gets its own decision.

sections.html:
This section is not legal advice. Laws differ between countries, change often, and are reinterpreted by regulators and courts; ask your company's privacy counsel before you rely on any of it. What follows is the state of the main rules as of November 2026, from this course's research, so you know which engineering requirements are already here and which are coming.

The GDPR has applied in the EU since 25 May 2018. Besides the principles in the last section, three articles turn into engineering work. Article 17 gives people the right to erasure of their personal data "without undue delay", with exceptions (data a company must keep by law, such as financial records, among them). Article 22 covers automated decisions, as in the Uber case. And the regulators' 2025 coordinated action on the right to erasure, published by the European Data Protection Board on 18 February 2026, says how well companies manage it. 32 data protection authorities took part, and 764 companies and other organizations answered. The EDPB rated compliance "average". Recurring problems included no documented erasure procedure, retention periods that were hard to define, deletion in backups (raised by half of the authorities), and anonymization used as a substitute for deletion. Where backups can't be edited, organizations should keep a record of erasure requests and apply it again whenever they restore, and they should be able to verify and demonstrate erasure.

Fines aren't final until the courts are done. In March 2026 a Luxembourg court annulled Amazon's €746 million GDPR fine, while upholding that the breaches happened, and sent the case back to the regulator.

Rule What it asks of systems Applies from
California: CCPA regulations on risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decision-making technology (ADMT) risk assessments for risky processing; audits on a staggered schedule 1 January 2026
California: the ADMT rules for significant decisions obligations for automated decisions about people 1 January 2027
California: Delete Act, the DROP platform registered data brokers process deletion requests from DROP at least every 45 days; $200 per request per day for failing 1 August 2026
EU AI Act, Article 50 tell people they are dealing with AI; label synthetic content (grace to 2 December 2026 for watermarking systems already on the market) 2 August 2026
EU AI Act, stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III: hiring, credit scoring and others) the high-risk obligations, logging and human oversight among them 2 December 2027
EU AI Act, AI in regulated products (Annex I) the same, for products such as medical devices and machinery 2 August 2028
EU Data Act access to the data of connected products; easier switching between cloud providers 12 September 2025; access by design for products placed on the market after 12 September 2026; switching charges abolished from 12 January 2027
India: DPDP Act core duties consent and data-fiduciary obligations 13 May 2027

The AI Act dates are new. The Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk deadlines back, so material written in 2024 or 2025 that says August 2026 for hiring and credit systems is out of date.

try.title: Match three features to the rules
steps: Your company runs in the EU and California. For each feature, name the rules from this section that apply and the date that matters. Remember this is a sketch for talking to counsel, not an answer.

1. A model that automatically freezes merchant accounts it scores as fraudulent. 2. A chatbot that answers cardholders' questions about disputed payments. 3. A screening model that ranks job applicants for the company's own engineering roles.
try.expect:
1. GDPR Article 22 if the merchants are individuals (sole traders), as in the Uber case: a fully automated freeze with significant effects needs a human who can review it, plus information about the logic. Under the California rules, an ADMT used for significant decisions has obligations from 1 January 2027. Freezing accounts for fraud isn't one of the AI Act's high-risk uses listed in this section, but check with counsel.

  2. EU AI Act Article 50, since 2 August 2026: tell people they are talking to an AI. The GDPR applies to the conversation data: purpose, retention, erasure.

  3. EU AI Act Annex III, hiring: high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027, not August 2026. GDPR Article 22 if no human makes the decision. California's ADMT rules for significant decisions, such as employment, from 1 January 2027. Mobley v. Workday shows the vendor of the model can be sued as well.

sections.html:
Almost everything in this course keeps data on purpose. A row deleted in PostgreSQL survives in the WAL, in old row versions until VACUUM removes them, in replicas until they replay the delete, and in last night's backup. Erasure has to reach every copy, and each copy has its own mechanism and its own clock:

  • A Kafka topic with time retention deletes whole segments, 7 days by default. On a compacted topic, a tombstone (a record with a null value) removes earlier values for the same key only, the active segment is never compacted, and max.compaction.lag.ms defaults to never forcing it. A customer's name inside an OrderPlaced event keyed by order ID is never removed by compaction at all (the Messaging and logs track's lesson on segments and compaction).
  • An event-sourced log (the Stream processing track) is meant to be kept for ever and replayed, so deleting events breaks the replay it exists for.
  • In an LSM store the tombstone hides a value at once, but the old bytes go only when compaction has merged them away at every level (the Storage engines track).
  • In an Iceberg table, a merge-on-read DELETE writes a delete file. The old Parquet file keeps the bytes until it is rewritten, then expire_snapshots removes every snapshot that still refers to it, and orphan cleanup runs (the Batch processing track's lesson on row-level changes). The time-travel window is also how long the deleted data can still be read.
  • Search indexes, caches and ML features each need the deletion to reach them, and a slow consumer can miss a tombstone altogether once delete.retention.ms (1 day by default) has removed it.
  • Backups need the EDPB's erasure record, applied again on restore.

Crypto-shredding handles the copies you can't edit. Encrypt each person's personal fields with a key that belongs to that person alone, and keep the keys in a separate store with short, separately managed backups. To erase someone, delete their key. Every copy of their ciphertext, wherever it is (topics, the lakehouse, old backups of the events), becomes unreadable at once, and the log still replays: in the lab, one customer's 24 events go from 24 decryptable to 0, every merchant total stays the same, and their row in the view shows [erased]. Then restore the key store from a backup taken before the request, and all 24 are readable again, unless the restore applies the erasure ledger.

Is that erasure in law? Nobody has settled it. The ciphertext still exists, and this course's research found no EDPB statement accepting key destruction as erasure. Commentary on the EDPB's 2025 guidelines on blockchains reports that they treat deleting a key as making data unreadable only until the encryption can be broken. What stays in the clear (a customer token, amounts, merchants, times) may still identify the person if anyone can link the token, and the EDPB has warned against calling data anonymous when it is only pseudonymous. Treat crypto-shredding as a strong technical measure that makes erasure fast and complete across copies, and combine it with keeping personal data out of events where you can (store a reference, keep the data in a store you can delete from), keying personal-data topics by person with bounded compaction, expiring snapshots on a schedule, and a scan afterwards that shows the person is gone.

try.title: Erase one customer from a log that never changes
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It seeds 1,000 payment events by 50 customers with per-customer keys, erases cust-017, replays the log, then restores last night's key backup twice.
Predict the four decryptable numbers before it prints.
Which line of output would you show an auditor as proof of erasure, and what would they still ask about?

code.title: ShredDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val backup = keys.backup() // last night's backup of the key store erase(ana, keys, ledger) // forget the key, record the request val after = rebuild(store, keys) // replay the whole log keys.restore(backup, ErasureLedger()) // a restore that knows nothing keys.restore(backup, ledger) // a restore that re-applies erasures

try.expect:
1000 events, 8 merchants; cust-017 has 24 events
plaintext emails found in the raw log: 0

before: decryptable 24 of 24, row CustomerView(name=Customer 17, email=zz-plain-17@example.com, payments=24, totalCents=241487)
after:  decryptable 0 of 24, row CustomerView(name=[erased], email=[erased], payments=24, totalCents=241487)
events still in the log: 1000; merchant totals unchanged: true

restore the backup, no ledger:   decryptable 24 of 24
restore the backup, with ledger: decryptable 0 of 24

The log never held a plaintext email, and after the key is gone none of the 24 events can be decrypted, while all 1,000 events and every total survive the replay. The naive restore undoes the erasure completely; the one that applies the ledger keeps it. An auditor would accept decryptable 0 of 24 as evidence, and would then ask where else the key could be (caches, other backups, a KMS export) and whether the customer token still links to the person anywhere.

sections.h: What you can do on Monday
sections.html:
None of this needs a new platform. It needs a week of looking at systems you already run, with the questions this course taught you to ask. Seven things, in the order I'd do them:

  1. Draw the data map for one service you own: every place a customer's data is written, including topics, caches, search, the lakehouse, metrics, log lines and backups, and which copy is derived from which. Name the system of record.
  2. For each copy, write down how a deletion reaches it and how long that takes. That list is your real erasure time. Mark every copy with no answer.
  3. Hunt the defaults that keep data for ever: compacted topics with max.compaction.lag.ms untouched, Iceberg tables with no snapshot-expiry job, emails and card numbers in log lines, backups with no erasure record.
  4. Take personal data out of events where you can (a reference to a store you can delete from), or encrypt it with a key per person and keep the key store's backups short and separate.
  5. Add one audit from lesson 5: recompute one derived view from its log and diff it, and reconcile one boundary before it sends anything irreversible.
  6. For one automated decision, such as a card block or a payout hold, log its inputs, model version and reasons with the request ID, measure its error rates for the groups you are allowed to measure, and make sure a person can reach a human who can overturn it.
  7. Delete one dataset nobody uses. It is the cheapest privacy work there is.

This course started from a single idea: one system of record, and everything else derived from it. Every track since has been about keeping those copies right while machines fail, clocks drift, networks split and code has bugs: logs and replicas, partitions and transactions, consensus, streams and batch jobs. This last lesson adds that the records are about people, who can be harmed by a wrong copy, by a copy kept too long, or by a decision nobody can explain. The engineering tools are the same ones: know where every copy is, derive them so you can rebuild them, check them, and make deletion as deliberate as writing. Start with the data map. Every other item on the list needs it, and most teams find a copy they didn't know they had.

try.title: Start the data map for one service
steps: Pick one service you know well. List every store it writes a customer's personal data to, directly or through something derived from it.
For each one, write how a deletion reaches it and roughly how long it takes. Leave a question mark where you don't know.
try.expect:
A sketch for a refunds service (yours will differ):

Copy How a deletion reaches it How long
refunds table in Oracle (system of record) DELETE by customer ID, in the erasure job at once; redo logs and archive per retention
refund-events topic, delete policy time retention up to 7 days, plus segment roll time
customer-profile topic, compacted tombstone keyed by customer ID ? (max.compaction.lag.ms is the default)
search index for the support tool consumer deletes by ID on the tombstone seconds, if the consumer is less than 1 day behind
Redis cache TTL 1 hour
Iceberg table refunds_daily DELETE, then the weekly rewrite and expire_snapshots up to 12 days
nightly Oracle backups erasure record re-applied on restore ? (no process yet)
application logs ? (emails appear in two log lines) 30 days

The question marks are the work: the compacted topic needs a bounded compaction lag, the backups need an erasure record, and the log lines need the emails removed. Most teams find at least one copy they didn't know about, often a log line or an analytics export.

analogy: A doctor's practice with paper files. The patient's main file sits in one cabinet, the system of record, but copies spread: a referral letter at the hospital, a page in the billing office, an X-ray at the lab, a line in the appointment book, the photocopies in last year's archive boxes. A patient who asks to have their records destroyed is asking about all of them, and shredding the main file handles one. Crypto-shredding is putting every copy in a locked envelope whose only key the practice holds, so burning the key makes every envelope useless at once, even in archive boxes nobody can find. The analogy breaks in two places. Paper copies don't multiply themselves, while every consumer of a log makes another copy without anyone deciding to. And a locked envelope is still an envelope: whether a court treats a burned key as a destroyed record is the open question in this lesson.
world: Payments engineering is where these rules bite first. Card data falls under PCI DSS, which already forces you to know where every card number lives; the same data map, extended to names, emails, IP addresses and device IDs, is the start of erasure. A fraud model that freezes a merchant or blocks a cardholder is an automated decision with significant effects: log its inputs, model version and reason codes with the request ID, as lesson 5 suggested, route the decisions people contest to a human queue whose staff can overturn them, and monitor false positives per segment. In Kafka, key personal-data topics by customer ID, set max.compaction.lag.ms and segment.ms to your erasure deadline, and keep names and emails out of events keyed by anything else. Keep per-customer data keys in a KMS or Vault and give the key store its own short backup policy with an erasure record re-applied on restore. Remember that a payments company also has legal duties to keep transaction records for years, so erasure there means removing what you are not obliged to keep, not everything.
mistake: Treating erasure as a DELETE in the main database. People do it because that is the only copy they designed; the others (topics, caches, search, the lakehouse, analytics exports, backups, log lines) grew around it. The deleted customer then lives on in a compacted topic whose tombstone never comes, in an Iceberg snapshot kept for time travel, and in last month's backup, which a restore brings back. The fix is to design erasure like any other derived-data flow: a data map of every copy, a deletion path and a deadline for each, crypto-shredding or references for the copies you can't edit, an erasure record that every restore applies again, and a scan afterwards that proves the person is gone.

worked.title: Erasure time for one customer, copy by copy

steps.say: The request arrives. The erasure job deletes the customer's rows in the system of record and writes a tombstone for their key to the compacted customer-profile topic.
steps.code:
t = 0      DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 'cust-017'
           produce("customer-profile", key = "cust-017", value = null)

steps.say: The compacted topic: the tombstone sits in the active segment, which is never compacted. With segment.ms at its 7-day default on a quiet topic, nothing can be cleaned until the segment rolls.
steps.code:
segment.ms            = 604800000             (7 days)
max.compaction.lag.ms = 9223372036854775807   (never forced)
worst case: the old value is readable for days, with no deadline

steps.say: Set both to the erasure deadline you committed to, and the cleaner has to get there in time. The tombstone itself stays for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default), so every consumer has a day to see it.
steps.code:
segment.ms            = 86400000    (1 day)
max.compaction.lag.ms = 172800000   (2 days)
delete.retention.ms   = 86400000    (1 day)

steps.say: The Iceberg table: the DELETE writes a delete file at once, but the bytes remain in old Parquet files. A weekly job rewrites the data files, and a daily job expires snapshots older than 5 days.
steps.code:
day 0   DELETE FROM refunds_daily WHERE customer_id = 'cust-017'
day 7   rewrite_data_files   (new files without the rows)
day 12  expire_snapshots     (the last snapshot that points at the old files is now 5 days old)
worst case: about 12 days, plus orphan-file cleanup

steps.say: The events were crypto-shredded, so they are unreadable as soon as the key is gone. The total is set by the slowest copy, so that is where to work.
steps.code:
event log (key deleted)       at once
customer-profile topic        within 2 days (after tuning)
Iceberg table                 about 12 days
backups                       on the next restore, via the erasure record

lab.title: Crypto-shred a customer from an immutable event log
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. 9 tests run and all fail with NotImplementedError, because seeding the store already needs encryption. Events.kt is finished: the event, the store that encrypts on append, and the seeded customers.

In Gcm.kt, write seal and open with the JDK's javax.crypto (AES/GCM/NoPadding, a 128-bit tag, the subject's bytes as associated data). The first two tests check the round trip and that a wrong key or subject fails.
In Keys.kt, write forget (remove the key and zero its bytes) and restore. Read the test restoring last night's key backup brings the erased customer back first: it shows why restore needs the ledger.
In Projection.kt, write rebuild and decryptable. A subject with no key is [erased]; a record that fails its tag while its key exists must throw.
Run all the tests until they pass. Then look at the test with the corrupted record and explain why it must fail loudly instead of showing [erased].
hints: seal: Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"), then init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv)), updateAAD(aad) and doFinal(plaintext). open is the same with DECRYPT_MODE.
restore: clear the map, put a copy of each backed-up key, then call forget for every subject in erased.subjects.
rebuild: keys.lookup(e.subject) is null for an erased subject. Don't wrap Gcm.open in runCatching there; in decryptable you may, since it only counts.

drill.title: Erasure and accountability, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write the steps of a right-to-erasure handler for a system with an event log, a key store with backups and a compacted topic; (2) list three things a system needs so that an automated decision can be contested; (3) give the EU AI Act date for high-risk hiring and credit-scoring systems, and the date Article 50 transparency started; (4) say in one sentence why crypto-shredding's legal status is open.

answer.html:
(1) delete the person's rows in the system of record
    forget their data key, and write their ID into the erasure ledger
    produce a tombstone for their key on the compacted topic (with a bounded
    max.compaction.lag.ms and segment.ms) so every consumer deletes too
    on any restore: restore the keys, then forget everyone in the ledger
    afterwards: scan every store for the person's identifiers and record the result
(2) a record of each decision: inputs, model version, reasons, request id;
    a human review queue with the power to overturn;
    a way for the person to see why, contest it and correct the data used
(3) 2 December 2027 (Annex III, after the Digital Omnibus on AI);
    Article 50 transparency from 2 August 2026
(4) the ciphertext still exists, and no regulator has said that destroying the
    key counts as erasing the data

recap: Models learn from records of past decisions, so proxies such as postcodes carry bias in after the group column is removed (COMPAS: 44.9% against 23.5% false positives; Optum: 17.7% against 46.5%). Measure error rates per group, and watch for feedback loops.

Automated decisions need accountability built into the system: a record of inputs, model version and reasons, human review with the power to overturn, and a way to contest. The Dutch regulator fined Uber €824,990,000 for automated deactivations without it (August 2026, under appeal).

Privacy is a decision right, consent is weaker than it looks, and personal data is a liability: 23andMe's genetic data was sold in bankruptcy for $305 million. Minimize, limit purposes, and give every dataset a retention period.

As of November 2026: GDPR erasure and automated-decision rules, the EDPB's findings on erasure in backups, California's 2026 regulations and the Delete Act's DROP, the AI Act's high-risk dates moved to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028, and the Data Act. This is not legal advice.

Erasure must reach every copy: topics, compaction, LSM tombstones, Iceberg snapshots, derived views and backups. Crypto-shredding makes copies you can't edit unreadable at once, a restore must re-apply the erasure record, and whether key destruction counts as erasure in law is still open.

explain.prompt: A product manager says: "We store everything in an event log so we can replay it. GDPR erasure is the legal team's problem, and anyway we delete the customer row." Explain why erasure is an engineering problem in this design and what you would build.
explain.answer: Deleting the customer row erases one copy. The same person's data is in every event in the log, which we keep so we can replay it, and in everything derived from it: the topics, the search index, the caches, the lakehouse table with its snapshots, and the backups of all of them. A request to erase has to reach each copy, and each has a different mechanism and deadline, so it is a dataflow problem like any other in our system. I would build a data map of every copy, then encrypt personal fields in events with a key per customer, so that deleting the key makes every copy of those events unreadable at once while the replay still works for totals. Personal-data topics would be keyed by customer with bounded compaction, the lakehouse would get scheduled rewrites and snapshot expiry, and the key store would get its own short backups plus an erasure ledger that every restore applies again. Afterwards a scan proves the person is gone, since the regulators ask us to demonstrate erasure. The legal team decides what we must keep and for how long; whether we can do it is ours. And none of this is legal advice: counsel should confirm whether key destruction is enough for our case, because that question is still open.

deeper.html:
Why fairness has no single number. In the COMPAS debate, the tool's maker answered ProPublica that its scores were equally predictive for both groups: among people given the same score, about the same share reoffended. ProPublica's numbers were about something else: the error rates among people who did not reoffend. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017) showed that when the groups' underlying rates differ, a score generally can't satisfy both definitions at once. That is a property of the arithmetic, not of one model, so a team has to choose which errors it cares about, say so, and measure them.

Erasure costs performance. Shastri and colleagues benchmarked what GDPR-style features (per-record metadata, timely deletion, access logs) do to databases such as Redis and PostgreSQL (PVLDB, 2020). Design them in early; retrofitting an erasure path onto a system built to keep everything is far harder than keeping a customer's data in one partition or under one key from the start.

Where to read the law itself. The GDPR is short enough to read in an evening, and its Articles 5, 17, 22 and 25 (data protection by design and by default) are the ones engineers meet. The EDPB publishes its guidelines and its coordinated-action reports, and the CPPA publishes California's regulations in full. Read them with counsel, not instead of counsel.

The ethical framing of this lesson, data as a liability and privacy as a decision right, follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 14; the cases, numbers and legal dates are from 2025 and 2026 sources.
